title: SpaceXAI and Cursor open Grok Bot public beta — always-on AI teammates that each get their own cloud computer
subtitle: The joint beta ships to Mac, iOS, PC and Linux with agents that sign into a user's real apps and finish multi-step work end-to-end, previewing the merged company's answer to ChatGPT Agent and Claude Cowork.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: SpaceXAI and Cursor opened Grok Bot to public beta on August 11 — a set of persistent AI agents that each run on a dedicated cloud computer, log into a user's own SaaS apps, and complete multi-step jobs without constant supervision. The beta is available on macOS, iOS, Windows and Linux, with Android to follow; access is bundled into three existing subscriptions — SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra and Cursor Teams Premium — while the two companies finish merging. Elon Musk said on last week's earnings call that the next-generation Grok 4.6 model will land later this week.

The interesting design choice is not the agent itself but the compute unit behind it. Rather than call APIs on the user's behalf, each Grok Bot gets its own persistent sandboxed desktop in the cloud and drives real applications through their real UIs — the same posture Google's Gemini Spark took when it moved from a remote managed browser to controlling the user's Chrome. That side-steps missing APIs and lets the bot handle whatever the user can, which is the point of an 'AI teammate' pitch, but also inherits every failure mode of UI automation: brittle selectors, session drift and prompt-injection from any page the bot loads.

The launch lands three months into SpaceX's $60B all-stock acquisition of Anysphere, Cursor's parent, and is the first joint product from the combined engineering teams. It slots into a crowded field — OpenAI's ChatGPT Agent, Anthropic's Claude Cowork, and Google's Gemini Spark all sell a version of the same 'delegate-a-task' proposition — and each is racing to prove its agent is the one an enterprise can actually trust with a company login. Access-tier bundling with Cursor is the tell that the go-to-market is developers first, general knowledge workers later.

For learners: watch how each vendor answers the same three questions — where does the agent's compute live, whose credentials does it use, and who is liable when it mis-clicks a payment page. The answers explain why Grok Bot requires manual approval before a purchase, why Gemini Spark keeps social posts human-gated, and why enterprise pilots stall on the second question long before they stall on capability. Agent quality is now table stakes; access, identity and audit trails are where the market will actually be decided.
